e.t: This Hebrew word means “house,” functioning as a noun for a place or structure. It occurs four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in two verses in 2 Kings 10. In its recorded uses, it serves as the object of actions or speech, so the surrounding sentence identifies what kind of house is intended. Its precise reference depends on that context.

Bariah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament Hebrew text, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 3:22, and is rendered “Bariah.” Because the available information identifies it only as a name and does not provide an explicit definition, its meaning cannot be expanded beyond that proper-name function. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “lord,” functioning as a title for someone recognized as having authority over others. Its two Old Testament occurrences are both in Genesis 27, where it is connected with blessing, bowing, and the expectation of service. The word therefore presents its referent as one who stands in a position of rule or honor, rather than merely naming an ordinary person. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to “Geber,” a personal name rather than a general description or action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:19, and the English rendering preserves it as a name. Because it functions as a name, its basic meaning is to identify a particular person; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in the passage. The word itself does not provide a broader common meaning in the available record.

This Hebrew noun refers to “soothsayers”—people identified in Daniel as a group whose supposed insight was sought in matters beyond ordinary human knowledge. It appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel. The word is used as a designation for these people rather than as an action or description of an event. Its repeated association with other advisers shows its role as a name for one recognized class of interpreters in the royal setting.

The Hebrew word means “standard,” referring to a visible marker used to identify and organize a group. It is a noun, appearing mainly in Numbers, where standards are associated with Israelite groups as they camp and set out. The word occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its use in Song of Songs shows that its basic sense extends beyond the camp arrangement. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: Zimran is a personal name, referring to a man named Zimran in the Hebrew Scriptures. The name appears twice in the Old Testament corpus, both times in genealogical passages that record family descent. It is associated with birth or begetting and functions as the name of an individual rather than a general description or action. Its occurrences are Genesis 25:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:32.

This Hebrew verb means “flood.” It describes water as an action rather than naming the water itself. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms: Psalm 77:17 and Psalm 90:5. Its use is associated with water and the forceful movement expressed by flooding. The surrounding verse determines the precise picture in each passage, but the central idea remains water flooding.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “breast,” naming a body part. In the Old Testament passages where it occurs, it refers to the breast connected with sacrificial offerings and with the portion presented, lifted, or given according to God’s command. It occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. Its precise significance in a particular passage depends on the surrounding instructions.

This word refers to Hamath Rabbah, a named place mentioned in Amos 6:2. It functions as a geographical name rather than a general description or action word. The name appears twice within the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both occurrences being in Amos 6:2. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the place being named. Scripture presents it alongside other named locations in the same verse.

The Hebrew word means “moles,” a plural noun naming the animals referred to by the word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament data, at Isaiah 2:20. In a sentence, it functions as a concrete noun rather than expressing an action or quality. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

This Hebrew word means “beetle.” It is a noun used as the name of a particular creature rather than as an action, quality, or description. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Leviticus 11:22. Since the available lexical support identifies it simply as “beetle,” that is the clearest ordinary meaning without adding a more specific identification. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its treatment of the named creature.

“Ibhar” is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than as a common word describing an action, object, or quality. It appears three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, and each occurrence is rendered “Ibhar.” The name occurs in passages recording David’s sons. No additional ordinary meaning is established for this name in the available lexical material.

This Hebrew word means “sweat,” referring to bodily moisture. It names a physical substance rather than an action, person, or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 44:18. Since the word appears only once and the verse text is not provided here, its basic lexical meaning can be stated clearly, while its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: Jokshan is a personal name, rendered “Jokshan.” It identifies a person in the genealogical records of Genesis and 1 Chronicles rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across three verses. Its recorded relationships place it within birth and family lineage statements, helping readers recognize it as an individual named in the ancestry of Abraham’s family. The precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Jerimoth, also rendered “Jeremoth,” is a personal name used for several individuals in the Old Testament. It does not function here as a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears 15 times across 14 Old Testament verses, especially in genealogical and historical lists. Because the same name is associated with more than one person, the surrounding passage is needed to identify which Jerimoth or Jeremoth is intended in a particular verse.

This word means “writing,” referring to words set down in written form. It is used in the Hebrew portions of Ezra and Daniel, where it can name writing itself or function in reference to what has been prescribed in writing. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, including ten occurrences in Daniel and two in Ezra. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “lion” or “lioness,” naming the animal itself. It functions as a concrete animal term in the Old Testament, appearing 14 times across 14 verses. Its uses include passages in Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Job, and other books, where the surrounding context determines whether the animal is presented as male or female. The word’s central meaning remains the wild feline known for strength and danger, rather than an abstract quality or action.

This Hebrew word means “hundred,” referring to a quantity of one hundred. It functions as a number word, stating how many people, animals, or items are being counted in a passage. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs eight times, concentrated in three verses in Ezra and Daniel. Its basic meaning remains numerical; the surrounding verse determines what the hundred is measuring.

This Hebrew word means “ready.” It is a descriptive word, used to identify the state of the person or thing being discussed. Within the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs four times, once each in Ezra, Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. The word’s exact force in a passage is determined by its surrounding sentence and context. The word alone does not replace that contextual reading.

This Hebrew noun means “besom,” a sweeping implement used to clear away dirt or debris. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 14:23, so it is a rare, concrete word rather than a term used broadly for ideas, actions, or character. It names the tool itself; the surrounding passage is needed to determine the significance of its use in that verse.

This Hebrew word functions as “it,” pointing to a thing already understood in the sentence rather than naming that thing again. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Leviticus: Leviticus 1:15 and 5:8. Because no explicit definition is available here, its clearest supported meaning is this pronoun-like reference. Its precise role in each verse depends on the surrounding wording, but it consistently identifies the object under discussion.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “threshold,” the entrance boundary or step at the base of a doorway. It refers to a defined place people cross when entering or leaving a building. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including descriptions of thresholds associated with the temple and other structures. Its use at a worship setting shows that the word can identify a significant place at the entrance of a sacred area, while its central meaning remains the doorway’s threshold.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “settings”—the crafted holders or fittings used with valuable ornamental pieces. It appears especially in the instructions and construction of the priestly garments, where these settings are made, attached, and given a defined place in the work. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with most occurrences in Exodus and one later occurrence in Psalms. Its repeated use in Exodus shows a specific term for an ornamental setting rather than a general object or decoration.

e.h: A Word for Comparison or Proverb
e.t: This Hebrew word expresses comparison or a proverb-like saying. It can describe something as “like” something else, drawing attention to a likeness or comparison. It can also refer to “proverbs,” pointing to concise sayings that communicate wisdom or a pointed observation. The word occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with examples in Numbers, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force depends on whether the sentence is making a comparison or referring to a proverb or saying.

The Hebrew word means “before.” It is a relational word: it places a person, object, or action in a position of reference to another person or thing. In ordinary reading, it can indicate that something is situated before another, or that an action occurs with another person as its point of reference. This word occurs 150 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force is determined by the sentence and surrounding passage.

This Hebrew verb means “wave.” It describes an action in which something is moved or presented with a waving motion. It is used especially in passages about offerings and sacred objects, where an item is waved before the LORD as part of worship. The word occurs 37 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including repeated instructions concerning priests and offerings. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being waved and the surrounding command.

This Hebrew verb means “come.” It expresses movement toward a place or person, or arrival, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Kings 6:9, so its wider range of use cannot be established from repeated occurrences. The available rendering supports “come” as its ordinary English sense. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the action being described.

This Hebrew verb means “cast.” It describes an action performed by a subject, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and 2 Kings. Its precise force depends on what the subject acts upon and the surrounding sentence. Thus, readers should understand it as an action word whose particular expression is clarified by each passage’s context.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “tender.” It describes something young, delicate, or newly developing rather than mature and hardened. In its three occurrences, all in the Song of Solomon, it refers to a stage of growth associated with vines and other flourishing life. The word appears in Song of Solomon 2:13, 2:15, and 7:13, so its meaning is especially connected with tender growth in poetic imagery. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word expresses what someone says as an authoritative command or directive—something spoken for another person to carry out. It is used 71 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, mostly in Daniel, with additional occurrences in Ezra and Jeremiah. Its normal function is verbal: it presents speech that gives an order, instruction, or ruling rather than merely describing an idea. The precise force in any particular verse depends on who speaks and how the surrounding sentence presents the command.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its basic sense is “times”. In Daniel, it serves as the time-related term in a sentence. The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew text represented here, all in Daniel, and English renderings commonly use “times.” Whether it refers to one time or more than one depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It directs attention to the time-related aspect of what is being said.

e.t: “Og” is a personal name, referring to the king identified in the Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but names one particular ruler who appears in Israel’s accounts of battles, territory, and conquered kings. This Hebrew name occurs 22 times in the Old Testament, including repeated references in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and the Psalms. Its consistent rendering is “Og.”

Azrikam is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify particular men rather than to describe an object, action, or quality. It appears six times in the Old Testament, each time referring to a person in genealogical, family, or community records. The name is rendered consistently as “Azrikam,” so its normal function is as a proper name. The available references span 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah, but the name itself does not provide enough information to determine each person’s character or role.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “sheaf,” referring to a gathered bundle of cut grain or a measured portion of grain. In Exodus, it names the measured amount of manna that each person was to gather, and a preserved portion was kept as a witness to God’s provision. Elsewhere, the word is connected with grain left in the field for the needy to gather. It occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, describing both a measured provision and grain available for harvest or collection.

This Hebrew word means “smoke,” referring to the visible vapor associated with burning or rising heat. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and the Psalms. In most recorded renderings, it is translated “smoke,” while one occurrence uses it in a different sentence role. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and sentence.

e.t: Paran is a proper name for a place. It is rendered “Paran” and refers to a location mentioned in the Old Testament, including places associated with the journeys and movements of biblical people. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 10 verses. Because it is a place name rather than a descriptive term, its basic meaning is the location itself; the surrounding passage identifies what happened there or who traveled through it.

This Hebrew word means “snared,” describing someone or something caught in a trap and unable to escape freely. It functions as a word describing a trapped condition rather than naming the trap itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 42:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is being caught and held fast.

This Hebrew word refers to an unspecified person or thing, functioning in English like “such.” It points to someone or something without identifying it by name, so its precise reference comes from the surrounding sentence. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once each in Ruth, 1 Samuel, and 2 Kings. Its use is therefore limited but consistent: it serves as a general designation when a specific name or identity is not given.

This Hebrew verb describes something flowing outward, spreading, or overflowing. Its central idea is movement that goes beyond a contained place rather than remaining still. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, with the approved meanings “flowed” and “overflow.” These uses point to water or another substance moving in abundance or passing beyond its boundaries. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding context, but the word consistently presents active outward flow.

The Hebrew word means “hunters,” referring to people who hunt. It is a plural noun, so it identifies more than one person rather than an action or quality. This word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 16:16. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete: people identified by hunting. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes someone being attired—being dressed or clothed for a particular setting. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including one occurrence in Leviticus 16:4 and two in Isaiah 22:18. Its wording functions as an action or description connected with how someone is dressed, rather than naming a garment itself. The precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew verb means “gathered.” It describes people or things being brought together into one group or place. The action may involve a community, an army, or objects collected for a purpose, depending on the surrounding passage. It occurs 127 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it commonly expresses the assembling of people or things rather than a single rare event. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being gathered and why.

This Hebrew verb means “gathered.” It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality, presenting something as having been gathered. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in Song of Songs. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, since the verse text is not included here. The word is therefore best understood as expressing the action of gathering in these two occurrences.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “fear.” It names the experience or condition of fear rather than describing an action. In the Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 49:24, so its normal meaning is supported by that single occurrence and its rendering there. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to fear as an inner response or state.

The Hebrew word means “feebleness,” identifying a condition of diminished strength. It describes a state rather than an action, person, or place. This word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Jeremiah 47:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the larger context. Its central idea remains a condition of feebleness.

It occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across four verses, and functions as a descriptor rather than an action or command. Its appearances are connected with spoken communication, including requests about what language should be used and speech heard in a royal setting. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Shobab.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs four times, each time as a name in genealogical or family records connected with birth or begetting. Its precise significance as a name is not established by the available lexical information, so “Shobab” is the supported meaning and ordinary use. The name appears in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “scourge,” referring to an instrument or means of severe punishment. It functions as a noun, naming something used to inflict painful discipline or affliction. In the Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, including passages about rulers threatening harsh treatment and passages describing overwhelming trouble. Its use can be literal or describe a force that brings distress, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise sense.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “drunken.” It describes a condition or state rather than naming a person or an action. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, so its meaning is tied to a specific biblical vocabulary rather than frequent everyday usage. In one recorded rendering, it is translated “drunken,” which supports understanding the word as describing a person or people affected by drunkenness. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “eight,” the number that follows seven and represents a quantity of eight objects, people, or units. It is a counting word used throughout the Old Testament, appearing 109 times across 105 verses. Its use ranges from counting people and generations to describing measurements and appointed periods. The surrounding words determine what is being counted, but the word itself consistently identifies the quantity eight.

This Hebrew word refers to “showers,” meaning rainfall that comes down from above. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:2, so its normal lexical range is represented by that single occurrence. The word functions as a noun, naming the falling rain rather than describing an action or person. Its precise force in Deuteronomy 32:2 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the basic meaning is clear: showers of rain.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to those or that which is left after others have been removed, defeated, or lost. Its approved meaning clue is “remain,” functioning as a term for what continues to exist. In the Old Testament, it occurs 29 times, often in passages describing people left alive after judgment or military conflict. The surrounding context determines whether it refers to a person, group, or remainder in a particular verse.

This Hebrew word refers to young cattle, rendered as “bullocks” or “bulls.” It is a noun used for actual animals, especially in lists of offerings or supplies. The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Daniel. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete: male cattle suitable for use in worship or other significant settings. The surrounding passage determines the particular purpose of the animals, but the word itself identifies the cattle rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word means “misused.” It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, at Genesis 27:12 and 2 Chronicles 36:16. Its use points to the idea of something being misused, but the precise force in either verse must be understood from the surrounding wording and passage.

e.t: “Tirzah” is a proper name used in the Old Testament for a woman and for a place. It identifies individuals or a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Numbers and continuing through Song of Songs. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage: in some occurrences it names a person, while in others it names a city.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Beer,” referring to a place. It functions as a noun rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Numbers 21:16 and once in Judges 9:21. Its use in these passages identifies a location connected with movement and with an event involving giving. The precise significance of the place in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes acting “treacherously”—conduct marked by betrayal or unfaithfulness toward another person. It functions as a verb, expressing what someone does rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 49 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Exodus through Malachi, showing that this is a recurring description of human conduct. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or relationship being described.

This Hebrew word means “trust.” It describes placing confidence in someone or something and functions in sentences as the action or state of trusting. In the Old Testament, it is used broadly for reliance expressed toward people, rulers, or God. It occurs 120 times in the Hebrew Bible, with especially frequent use in the Psalms, showing that trust is a recurring way Scripture describes dependence and confidence. Its precise force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding context.
